title: FCC approves Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery merger
seoTitle: FCC Approves Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery Merger
subtitle: Understand what motivated the approval and what limits are imposed on foreign investment
excerpt: The FCC authorized the merger between Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery after analyzing the participation of investors from countries such as.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
The FCC's approval of the merger between Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery gained prominence in searches after the agency completed its review of foreign ownership in the new group. The official FCC document indicates that the decision was made based on the public interest.

Why the FCC reviewed the merger

The FCC has the authority to analyze transactions involving foreign ownership of over 25% in companies holding broadcast licenses. In this case, foreign capital in the combined group would reach 49.5%, with 38.5% coming from investment funds in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi.

Conditions imposed on foreign investment

The regulatory body included in its decision that if the voting share of foreign investors exceeds 25% or if there is a change in the approved holdings, a new FCC authorization will be required. Furthermore, foreign investors will have no voting control or governance rights.

Guarantees of national control

Paramount reported that the Ellison family and RedBird will retain the majority of voting shares, ensuring that no external participant exerts decision-making power. The company also presented an agreement that protects data and restricts access for foreign investors.

Reactions within the FCC

Anna Gomez, the sole Democrat on the FCC, questioned the extent of foreign ownership and requested that the matter be submitted to a full vote by the commission, arguing that the decision was made at the staff level without broad debate.

Impact of the approval

With the approval, the merger can move forward, consolidating the media assets of both groups under the majority control of American shareholders. The decision also demonstrates how the FCC balances national security interests and openness to foreign capital in major media transactions.

With information from Deadline.
